On the eve of Passover, Reb Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev went out into the street of his town. He met the local smuggler and asked whether he could get him some contraband tobacco and embroidered brocades. The Polish-Russian border was closed, and smuggling was a capital offense. In less than an hour, the goods were in the Rebbe's hands.

The tzaddik then began walking the streets of Berditchev, knocking on doors. When the owner opened, the Rabbi asked him for a piece of pumpernickel bread. In every case the householder was shocked and dismayed that the Rebbe would accuse him of having chametz in the house. He calmed their worries and went on his way.

After several hours of this, Reb Levi Yitzchak went to the shul, threw open the doors of the holy ark and called out: "Master of the Universe! The borders are heavily guarded, and yet in less than an hour this contraband was in my hands. Your people, out of love for You, are embarrassed by the mere suggestion that they have chametz, and there are no guards at all. Who is like Your people Israel! The czar needs guards and police, and You need none."
source: Chabad.org, 'Minister for the Defense' (Rabbi Elisha Greenbaum) (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Cantonists' Ne'ilah
text:
Reb Mordechai, a chassid of the third Rebbe of Chabad, Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Lubavitch (1789-1866), had been sent by his Rebbe to wander the Russian countryside, going from town to town to inspire the Jews scattered there with the teachings of Chassidism. One day, the day before Yom Kippur, he arrived in a town in the middle of nowhere, only to hear that all its Jews, about a hundred in all, had left the day before for the city of Vitebsk, to pray in the large synagogue there on the Day of Atonement.

Suddenly, a few hours before the holiest day of the year, he found himself without a minyan, the quorum of ten Jews needed for communal prayer. "You won't find any Jews here, Rabbi," one of the townspeople told him. "But about two hours away there's a small village of Cantonists. They're a strange bunch, but that's the closest thing to Jews you'll find around here now."

The Cantonists were Jews who, by decree of Czar Nicholas I, had been snatched from their families as young children for a 25-year term of "service" in the Czar's army, where every cruel means was used to force them to abandon Judaism. The few who survived came out decades later so broken in body and spirit that they could never live normal lives. So they lived together in little villages, apart from the rest of the world.

Reb Mordechai set out at once. After more than an hour he still saw nothing. Then, on the horizon, something appeared: a few old wooden houses. This must be the village. The first resident who saw the rabbi enter called the others, and in no time they were all lined up with shining faces, taking turns shaking the newcomer's hand. They were overjoyed. Such an honor, a real rabbi as their guest!

Then they stepped back, formed a sort of huddle and began whispering. They fell silent, looked at the rabbi again, and one of them stepped forward in great humility, cleared his throat and announced: "Excuse me, Rabbi, but we would be very honored if his excellency the Rabbi would honor us by leading the prayers of Yom Kippur." The others stood staring at him with wide, pleading eyes, nodding their heads. Reb Mordechai agreed, and the joyous handshaking began all over again. "We have only one condition," the man went on. "One of us leads Ne'ilah, the closing prayer of the holy day."

An hour later they were all seated in the solemn atmosphere of Yom Kippur in their little shul, listening to the beautiful, heartfelt prayers of the Chassidic rabbi. A very special feeling came over Reb Mordechai. He had never experienced a Yom Kippur like this. He had never been in such a minyan: Jews each of whom had been through hell, things he could never even dream of, only for the sake of G-d. He knew all the books and they knew nothing, yet he felt dwarfed by these simple folk.

His soul flowed into the prayers, and it seemed to him he had never sung so beautifully in his life. First Kol Nidrei, then the evening prayer; the following day he led the other three prayers and read twice from the Torah. Finally, at the end of the day, came their turn. It was time for Ne'ilah.

Reb Mordechai stepped back, took a seat with everyone else and waited to see what would happen. Why did they want this prayer for themselves? One of the Cantonists rose, took a few steps forward and stood at the podium, his back to the crowd. Then, before he began, he started unbuttoning his shirt and taking it off. Reb Mordechai was about to protest: you can't take your shirt off in the synagogue! But as the shirt fell from the man's shoulders, it revealed hundreds of scars, years upon years of deep scars, each one because the man had refused to forsake the G-d of Israel.

Reb Mordechai gasped, and tears ran down his face. The Cantonist raised his hands to G-d and said in a loud voice: "G-d, send us Moshiach! Redeem the Jewish people now! I'm not asking for the sake of our families, because we have no families. I'm not asking for the sake of our futures, because we have no futures. I'm not asking for the sake of our livelihoods, our comfort, our children or our reputations, because we have none of those things either. We are only asking: *Asei l'maan shemecha*, do it for Your sake!"

Then he put his shirt back on and began the prayer.
source: Chabad.org, 'The Cantonists' Minyan' (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Drought and the Missing Umbrellas
text:
The story is told of a community suffering from a severe drought. The elders proclaimed a day of prayer and fasting, in the hope of arousing G-d's compassion.

As they were about to enter the synagogue, a little girl turned to her father and said, "Daddy, you grown-ups don't really believe these prayers will help, do you?"

"Why do you say that?" asked the father.

"Well," said the little girl, "none of you brought umbrellas."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: The Power of a Tallis
text:
We hold our Shabbos services in a hotel, so it is not surprising that people find us, whether they are staying at the hotel or looked us up on the web. A few months ago I was walking to our "davening room," our shul, when a heavyset Israeli came running up to me, gave me a warm "Shalom Aleichem," and blurted out: "You must be from Chabad! I was sitting in the restaurant at a business meeting and noticed you walk by. I didn't want to lose you, so I ran after you to tell you I'll be coming to shul. And I especially want to share an unbelievable but true story with you.

"During the Yom Kippur War, I was in charge of a group of soldiers. We had tanks and heavy artillery supporting us. Yet the first two days of the war were a sheer disaster. We were completely overrun by the Egyptians. There we were in enemy territory: most of our group killed, the tanks destroyed, our communications cut off, our radios dead, and we were worn down, exhausted and beaten.

"Suddenly, in the distance, we saw Israeli flags waving in the breeze, and a group of Israeli tanks. We were saved! Israeli reserves had been sent to rescue us! We sprang to our feet and, with all the energy we could muster, ran as fast as we could toward the rescue team. But the sight that met our eyes was devastating: they were taking aim at us. They had mistaken us for Arabs because of our unkempt, unshaven, filthy appearance after two days of heavy fighting.

"Without wasting a moment, one of my soldiers pulled a tallis from his pack and ran straight toward the tanks, through flying bullets, waving it high in the air. That heroic act identified us as Jews, and he saved us all.

"Where did that tallis come from? It was his own. When we retreated he had salvaged it, together with his tefillin, and carried it with him. At the time I didn't want to pray, I didn't believe. But now, every time I see a tallis, I remember that I am alive today because of one."
source: JTA (1998), 'Remembering Yom Kippur War: survivor of Egyptian onslaught recalls hellish days of October' (Yossi Harel, Milano post, Bar Lev line)

title: How Poor We Are
text:
One day the father of a very wealthy family took his son on a trip to the country, to show him just how poor some people are. They spent a couple of days on the farm of a very poor family.

On the way home, the father asked, "Son, how was the trip?"

"It was great, Dad."

"Did you see how poor people can be?"

"Oh yeah," said the son.

"So what did you learn?"

The son answered, "I learned that we don't allow pets in our fancy house, but they have dogs and cats they enjoy very much. We have a pool that reaches to the middle of our garden, and they have a creek that has no end. We have imported Japanese lanterns in our garden, and they have the stars at night. We have a small piece of land to live on, and they have fields that go beyond our sight. We have servants who serve us, but they serve others. We have walls around our property to protect us; they have friends to protect them."

The father was speechless. Then his son added, "Thanks, Dad, for showing me how poor we are."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: The Captain Is My Father
text:
A boy was once playing by himself on the beach. A passerby stopped and asked why he didn't go and play with the other children at the far end of the beach.

The little boy answered that he was waiting for a boat to pass so that he could wave his flag to the captain.

"But no small boats pass this spot," said the man, "only a big tanker. So why don't you go and play with the other children?"

"No, that's exactly the boat I'm waiting for!" the boy said eagerly. "I'm waiting to wave my flag to the captain of that tanker. Then he'll wave a flag back to me."

"That's silly," said the man. "The captain of that ship is a very important person. I doubt he could even see you from that distance. In fact, I can't imagine why he would be looking in this direction at all."

"Oh, I know that not only will the captain be looking for me, he'll wave back to me," the child said confidently.

"How can you be so sure?"

"Because the captain is my father."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: Tess Buys a Miracle
text:
Tess was a precocious eight-year-old when she heard her Mom and Dad talking about her little brother, Andrew. All she knew was that he was very sick and that they were completely out of money. They were moving to an apartment complex next month, because Daddy didn't have the money for both the doctor bills and the house. Only a very costly surgery could save him now, and it looked as if there was no one to lend them the money. She heard Daddy say to her tearful mother, in a desperate whisper, "Only a miracle can save him now."

Tess went to her bedroom and pulled a glass jelly jar from its hiding place in the closet. She poured all the change out on the floor and counted it carefully. Three times, even. The total had to be exactly right; there was no room for mistakes.

Carefully placing the coins back in the jar and twisting on the cap, she slipped out the back door and made her way six blocks to Rexall's Drug Store, with the big red Indian Chief sign above the door. She waited patiently for the pharmacist to give her some attention, but he was too busy just then. Tess twisted her feet to make a scuffing noise. Nothing. She cleared her throat with the most disgusting sound she could muster. No good. Finally she took a quarter from her jar and banged it on the glass counter. That did it!

"And what do you want?" the pharmacist asked in an annoyed tone. "I'm talking to my brother from Chicago, whom I haven't seen in ages," he added, without waiting for an answer.

"Well, I want to talk to you about *my* brother," Tess answered back in the same annoyed tone. "He's really, really sick, and I want to buy a miracle."

"I beg your pardon?" said the pharmacist.

"His name is Andrew, and he has something bad growing inside his head, and my Daddy says only a miracle can save him now. So how much does a miracle cost?"

"We don't sell miracles here, little girl. I'm sorry, but I can't help you," the pharmacist said, softening a little.

"Listen, I have the money to pay for it. If it isn't enough, I'll get the rest. Just tell me how much it costs."

The pharmacist's brother was a well-dressed man. He stooped down and asked the little girl, "What kind of a miracle does your brother need?"

"I don't know," Tess replied, her eyes welling up. "I just know he's really sick and Mommy says he needs an operation. But my Daddy can't pay for it, so I want to use my money."

"How much do you have?" asked the man from Chicago.

"One dollar and eleven cents," Tess answered, barely audibly. "And it's all the money I have, but I can get some more if I need to."

"Well, what a coincidence," smiled the man. "A dollar and eleven cents: the exact price of a miracle for little brothers." He took her money in one hand, and with the other he took hold of her mitten and said, "Take me to where you live. I want to see your brother and meet your parents. Let's see if I have the kind of miracle you need."

That well-dressed man was a neurosurgeon. The operation was done without charge, and it wasn't long before Andrew was home again and doing well.

Mom and Dad were happily talking about the chain of events that had led them to this point. "That surgery," her Mom whispered, "was a real miracle. I wonder how much it would have cost?"

Tess smiled. She knew exactly how much a miracle cost: one dollar and eleven cents... plus the faith of a little child.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: Chanukah in Bergen-Belsen
text:
In the concentration camp of Bergen-Belsen, on the eve of Chanukah, a selection took place. Early in the morning, three German commandants, meticulously dressed in their festive black uniforms and in visibly high spirits, entered the men's barracks. They ordered the men to stand at the foot of their three-tiered bunks, and the selection began. No papers were checked; there was no roll call and no head count. One of the commandants simply lifted an index finger in his snow-white glove, pointed at a pale face, and pronounced the death sentence in a single word: "Come!"

Like a barrage of machine-gun fire came the commands: "Komme, komme, komme, komme." The men selected were marched outside, where S.S. men with rubber truncheons and iron prods awaited them. They kicked, beat and tortured their innocent victims, and when a tortured body no longer responded, the revolver was used. The random selection went on inside the barracks, and the massacre outside, until sundown. When the black angels of death departed, they left behind heaps of hundreds of tortured, twisted bodies.

Then Chanukah came to Bergen-Belsen. It was time to kindle the Chanukah lights. There was no jug of oil to be found, no candle in sight, and a menorah belonged to the distant past. Instead, a wooden clog, the shoe of one of the inmates, became the menorah; strings pulled from a camp uniform, the wick; and black camp shoe polish, the oil. Not far from the heaps of bodies, the living skeletons gathered to take part in the kindling of the Chanukah lights.

The Rabbi of Bluzhov lit the first light and chanted the first two blessings in his pleasant voice, and the festive melody was filled with sorrow and pain. When he came to the third blessing, he stopped, turned his head and looked around, as if searching for something. Then he turned back to the quivering little lights and, in a strong, reassuring, comforting voice, chanted the third blessing: "Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the Universe, Who has kept us alive, and sustained us, and enabled us to reach this season."

Among those present was a Mr. Zamietchkowski, one of the leaders of the Warsaw Bund. He was a clever, sincere man with a passion for discussing religion, faith and truth, and even in Bergen-Belsen that passion had not faded; he never missed an opportunity for such a conversation. As soon as the Rabbi of Bluzhov had finished the kindling, Zamietchkowski elbowed his way over to him and said: "Spira, you are a clever and honest person. I can understand your need to light Chanukah candles in these wretched times. I can even understand the historical note of the second blessing, 'Who performed miracles for our fathers in days of old, at this season.' But the fact that you recited the third blessing is beyond me. How could you thank G-d and say 'Who has kept us alive, and sustained us, and enabled us to reach this season'? How could you say it when hundreds of dead Jewish bodies are literally lying in the shadow of the Chanukah lights, when thousands of living Jewish skeletons are walking around this camp, and millions more are being massacred? For this you are thankful to G-d? For this you praise Him? This you call 'keeping us alive'?"

"Zamietchkowski, you are a hundred percent right," answered the rabbi. "When I reached the third blessing, I also hesitated and asked myself, what should I do with this blessing? I turned my head to ask the Rabbi of Zaner and the other distinguished rabbis standing near me whether I might indeed recite it. But just as I turned my head, I noticed that behind me a throng was standing, a large crowd of living Jews, their faces expressing faith, devotion and concentration as they listened to the kindling of the Chanukah lights.

"I said to myself: if G-d, blessed be He, has such a nation, that at times like these, when during the lighting of the Chanukah lights they see before them the heaps of bodies of their fathers, brothers and sons, and death looks out from every corner, if despite all that they stand in throngs and listen with devotion to the blessing 'Who performed miracles for our fathers in days of old, at this season'; if I was indeed blessed to see such a people, with so much faith and fervor, then I am under a special obligation to recite the third blessing."

Some years after liberation, the Rabbi of Bluzhov, then living in Brooklyn, New York, received regards from Mr. Zamietchkowski. Zamietchkowski had asked the son of the Skabiner Rabbi to tell Israel Spira, the Rabbi of Bluzhov, that the answer he gave him that dark Chanukah night in Bergen-Belsen had stayed with him ever since, and had been a constant source of inspiration in hard and troubled times.
source: Yaffa Eliach, 'Hasidic Tales of the Holocaust' (told by the Bluzhover Rebbe, Rabbi Israel Spira); retold by Ohr Somayach, Aish and others

title: What If I Were?
text:
A story is told of an old lady on a bus in Israel who overheard two girls gossiping about their friend, who had recently become engaged to a fine young man. To pass the time, they began listing their engaged friend's flaws and guessing how the groom would react when he discovered them. How would he react when he learned that she didn't know how to cook and had never washed a dish? How loving would he be when he found out that she couldn't save a penny, rarely brushed her teeth, and that her room was always a mess? They shrieked with laughter as they imagined the groom's reactions.

The old lady leaned over and said, "I couldn't help overhearing your conversation, and I'm glad I did. This young man is my grandson, and now that I know how terrible his bride is, I will encourage him to break off the engagement."

The girls were aghast. They had never imagined that their innocent chatter would bring such bitter results for their good friend. They stammered a hasty retraction, but the old lady interrupted them with a smile.

"I am not his grandmother," she said. "But what if I were?"
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: Can I Buy an Hour of Your Time?
text:
Sometimes we forget what life is really about.

A man came home from work late, tired and irritated, to find his five-year-old son waiting for him at the door.

"Daddy, may I ask you a question?"

"Yeah, sure. What is it?"

"Daddy, how much do you make an hour?"

"That's none of your business. Why do you ask such a thing?" the man said angrily.

"I just want to know. Please tell me, how much do you make an hour?" pleaded the little boy.

"If you must know, I make $20 an hour."

"Oh," the little boy replied, with his head down. Looking up, he said, "Daddy, may I please borrow $10?"

The father was furious. "If the only reason you asked is so you can borrow money to buy a silly toy or some other nonsense, then march yourself straight to your room and go to bed. Think about why you're being so selfish. I work long, hard hours every day and don't have time for this childish behavior."

The little boy quietly went to his room and shut the door. The man sat down and grew even angrier about his son's questions. How dare he ask such questions just to get some money?

After an hour or so, the man had calmed down and started to think. Maybe he had been a little hard on his son. Maybe there was something he really needed to buy with that $10; he really didn't ask for money very often. The man went to the boy's room and opened the door.

"Are you asleep, son?"

"No, Daddy, I'm awake."

"I've been thinking. Maybe I was too hard on you earlier. It's been a long day and I took out my aggravation on you. Here's the $10 you asked for."

The little boy sat straight up, smiling. "Oh, thank you, Daddy!" Then, reaching under his pillow, he pulled out some crumpled bills. Seeing that the boy already had money, the man started to get angry again. The little boy slowly counted out his money, then looked up at his father.

"Why do you want more money if you already have some?" the father grumbled.

"Because I didn't have enough, but now I do," the little boy replied. "Daddy, I have $20 now. Can I buy an hour of your time? Please come home early tomorrow. I would like to have dinner with you."
source: A parable, from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection

title: The Menorah in the Window
text:
Hashgacha pratis, Divine providence, is a major player in all of our lives. Sometimes it takes the bright burning lights of a menorah reuniting a family to help us see it.

Private Winneger was with the U.S. Army as it marched through Europe at the end of World War II. His unit was assigned to a European village, with orders to secure the town, search for any Nazis in hiding, and help the villagers in any way they could.

One night Winneger was on patrol when he saw a figure running through a field just outside the village. He shouted, "Halt or I'll shoot!" The figure ducked behind a tree. Winneger waited. Eventually the figure came out, and thinking Winneger was no longer nearby, went to a spot near a large tree and started to dig. Winneger waited until the digging was done and the figure was on the move again, then stepped out and shouted once more, "Halt or I'll shoot!" The figure ran. Winneger decided not to shoot but to catch the furtive figure, and he soon caught up and tackled it to the ground.

To his surprise, he found he had captured a young boy. An ornate menorah had fallen from the boy's hands in the scuffle. Winneger picked it up, and the boy tried to grab it back, shouting, "Give it to me! It's mine!" Winneger assured the boy that he was among friends; what's more, he himself was Jewish. The boy, who had just survived several years of the Holocaust and had been in a concentration camp, was mistrustful of all men in uniform. He had been forced to watch his father being shot. He had no idea what had become of his mother.

In the weeks that followed, Winneger took the boy, whose name was David, under his wing. As they grew closer, Winneger's heart went out to him, and he offered David the chance to come back with him to New York City. David accepted, and Winneger went through all the necessary paperwork and officially adopted him.

Winneger was active in the New York Jewish community. An acquaintance of his, a curator of the Jewish Museum in Manhattan, saw the menorah and told David it was a very valuable, historic European menorah that ought to be shared with the whole Jewish community. He offered David $50,000 for it. But David refused the generous offer, saying the menorah had been in his family for over 200 years and no amount of money could make him sell it.

When Chanukah came, David and Winneger lit the menorah in the window of their home in New York City. David went upstairs to his room to study, and Winneger stayed downstairs in the room with the menorah.

There was a knock at the door. Winneger opened it to find a woman with a strong German accent. She said that she had been walking down the street when she saw the menorah in the window. She had once had one just like it in her family and had never seen another like it. Could she come in and take a closer look? Winneger invited her in and said the menorah belonged to his son, who could perhaps tell her more about it. He went upstairs and called David down.

As David came down the stairs and saw her, he shrieked, "Mama!" As she set eyes on him, she burst into tears. She was reunited with the son she had thought had perished. They were the only surviving members of their family, and though each had believed the other was gone forever, they were brought together again, as the menorah provided yet another Chanukah miracle.
source: A well-known story; its details cannot be confirmed (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: Who Taught You How to Sin?
text:
A chassid once came to Rabbi Menachem Mendel of Kotzk, the Kotzker Rebbe, sobbing bitterly. "Rebbe, I have sinned. I have transgressed. Please teach me how to do teshuvah, how to return."

"Who taught you how to sin?" asked the Rebbe.

"No one taught me. I just saw an opportunity, seized the moment, and sinned."

"Then that is how you should return," said the Rebbe. "Just do it."
source: Chabad.org, 'Nasso: What Cannot Be Commanded' (story of the Kotzker Rebbe) (from Rabbi Labkowski's story collection)

title: The Shul I Won't Set Foot In
text: David was rescued after twenty years alone on a desert island. "How did you survive? How did you stay sane?" the rescuers asked as he showed them around. "I had my faith. My faith as a Jew kept me strong. Come." He led them to a small glen where a magnificent temple stood, built entirely of palm fronds, coconut shells and woven grass. The news cameras photographed everything, even a Torah made of banana leaves and written in octopus ink. "This took me five years to complete." "Amazing! And what did you do for the next fifteen years?" "Come with me." He led them to the far side of the island, where, in a shady grove, stood an even more beautiful temple. "This one took me twelve years!" "But sir," asked a reporter, "why did you build two temples?" "This is the temple I attend. That other place? Hah! I wouldn't set foot in that other temple if you paid me!"

title: The Custom Is to Argue
text: A young scholar from New York was invited to become the rabbi of a small, old community in Chicago. On his very first Shabbat a heated debate broke out over whether one should stand or sit during the reading of the Ten Commandments. The next day the rabbi visited 98-year-old Mr. Katz in the nursing home. "Mr. Katz, I'm asking you as the oldest member of the community," said the rabbi. "What is our synagogue's custom during the reading of the Ten Commandments?" "Why do you ask?" said Mr. Katz. "Yesterday we read the Ten Commandments. Some people stood, some people sat. The ones standing started screaming at the ones sitting to stand up, and the ones sitting started screaming at the ones standing to sit down..." "That," said the old man, "is our custom."

title: Bubbe Can Cook
text: Little Yossi and his family were having dinner at his bubbe's house. When everyone was seated, the food was served, and as soon as Yossi got his plate he started eating. "Yossi, please wait until we say the blessing," said his father. "I don't have to," Yossi replied. "Of course you have to," said his mother. "Don't we always say a blessing before eating at our house?" "Yes, but that's our house," Yossi explained. "This is Bubbe's house, and she knows how to cook."

title: You Be Rabbi Felder
text: Talia Rosenberg, a young mother, was making breakfast for her two little boys, Moishie, five, and Shmueli, three. They were arguing over who would get the first pancake. Hoping to teach them some good values, Talia asked them to think of their saintly rabbi, Rabbi Felder. "What do you think Rabbi Felder would do here? I think he would say, 'Let my brother have the first pancake.'" Moishie turned at once to Shmueli and said, "You be Rabbi Felder."

title: Try Not to Cry, Yossi
text: An old zaida was shlepping his einikel, his grandson, through the grocery store. The toddler was crying, and at times screaming at the top of his lungs. As the zaida walked up and down the aisles, people could hear him saying softly, "We're almost done, Yossi. Try not to cry, Yossi. Life will get better, Yossi." At the checkout he gently wiped the toddler's tears and said again, "Try not to cry, Yossi. We'll be home soon, Yossi." While he was paying, the toddler still crying, a young woman in line behind him said, "Sir, I think it's wonderful how sweet you're being to your little Yossi." The zaida blinked a couple of times and said, "My grandson's name is Yankele. I'm Yossi."

title: What Were the Grown-Ups Doing?
text: The Sunday school lesson had just ended, and the rabbi asked whether the children had any questions. Little David's hand shot up. "Yes, David? What would you like to ask?" "I have four questions, Rabbi. Is it true that after the children of Israel crossed the Red Sea, they received the Ten Commandments?" "Yes, David." "And the children of Israel also defeated the Philistines?" "Yes, David, that's true too." "And the children of Israel also fought the Romans and the Egyptians and built the Temple?" "Right again, David." "So my last question is, Rabbi: what were the grown-ups doing all this time?"

title: All the Kosher Restaurants Were Closed
text: Morris goes to the rabbi and says, "I committed a sin, and I want to know how I can repent." "What was the sin?" the rabbi asks. "It happened just once," Morris assures him. "I didn't wash my hands and say the blessing before eating bread." "Nu, if it really only happened once," says the rabbi, "that's not so terrible. Still, why didn't you wash and say the blessing?" "I felt awkward, Rabbi," says Morris. "You see, I was in a non-kosher restaurant." The rabbi's eyebrows go up. "And why were you eating in a non-kosher restaurant?" "I had no choice," says Morris. "All the kosher restaurants were closed." "And why were all the kosher restaurants closed?" "It was Yom Kippur."

title: Why Are You So Tired?
text: Yom Kippur was over, the fast was broken, and the rebbetzin dropped into an easy chair. "Oy! Am I tired!" The rabbi looked over at her. "During these High Holidays I had to lead five special services, go without food or drink, and give five sermons. Why are *you* so tired?" "My dear," she replied, "I also fasted and sat through all of it. But on top of that, every minute I had to sit in the front row, beam with pride and pretend to be impressed!"

title: Everything in My Wife's Name
text: A gabbai approaches a guest in shul and says, "I'd like to give you an aliyah. What is your name?" The man answers, "Esther bas Moshe." "No, I need *your* name," says the gabbai. "It's Esther bas Moshe," the man repeats. "How can that be your name?" "I've been having serious financial problems," the man explains, "so everything is in my wife's name."

title: Value for Money
text: A man and his ten-year-old son were visiting London, found an old synagogue and decided to go in for services. The father felt in his pockets, found only a pound coin, and gave it to his son to drop into the tzedakah box on the way in. When they left, the son asked, "Dad, what did you think?" The father grumbled, "The service was too long, the sermon was boring and the singing was off-key. What did you think, son?" "Daddy, I thought we did pretty well for a quid!"

title: Don't Want to Remind Him
text: A pious man who had reached the age of 105 suddenly stopped coming to synagogue. Alarmed by his absence after so many years of faithful attendance, the rabbi went to see him and found him in excellent health. "How come, after all these years, we don't see you at services anymore?" the rabbi asked. The old man lowered his voice. "I'll tell you, Rabbi," he whispered. "When I got to be 90, I expected G-d to take me any day. But then I got to be 95, then 100, then 105. So I figured G-d is very busy and must have forgotten about me, and I don't want to remind Him!"

title: Do You Have a Ticket?
text: An elegantly dressed man walks up the steps of a large temple on Rosh Hashanah. At the front door a security guard stops him. "Are you a member of this synagogue, sir?" "No." "Did you buy a ticket for the Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur services here?" "No, I did not." The guard is apologetic. "I'm sorry, but then I can't let you into the synagogue." The man is desperate. "But I have a very important message for Mr. Brian Goldstein. It's a matter of the greatest importance, in fact an emergency. You have to let me in to speak with him!" The guard relents. "OK, OK, I'll let you in. But if I catch you praying..."

title: Talking to a Brick Wall
text: An American journalist in Jerusalem heard about an old rabbi who had gone to the Kotel, the Western Wall, to pray twice a day, every day, for more than fifty years. To check out the story she went to the holy site, and there he was. She watched him pray for about 45 minutes, and when he turned to leave she approached him. "I'm Rebecca Smith from CNN. Sir, how long have you been coming to the Wall to pray?" "About 50 years," he told her. "That's amazing! What do you pray for?" "I pray for peace between Jews and Arabs. I pray for all the hatred to stop, and I pray for all our children to grow up in safety and friendship." "And how do you feel, sir, after doing this for 50 years?" "Like I'm talking to a brick wall!"

title: Kiddush or Kaddish
text: A young boy from a not-too-religious home comes back from his first day at Hebrew school, and his father asks what he learned. "We learned to say Kaddish, Papa." The father is not at all happy to hear this, so he runs down to the synagogue and confronts the rabbi. "Rabbi, what is this about teaching my son to say Kaddish? He shouldn't know about such things at so young an age. Besides, I'm a young man myself, in excellent health, and I expect to live a long time yet!" The rabbi answered, "First of all, it's not Kaddish, it's Kiddush! And secondly, you should only live so long until he learns it!"

title: Judging Favorably
text:
Moe and Lenny are strolling home from shul one Shabbat morning when a cab speeds past, with their friend Irving running frantically behind it, waving his arms. "Well," says Lenny, "I never imagined our good friend Irving was a Sabbath violator! Look at him running for that taxi."

"Wait a minute," says Moe. "Didn't you read that book I lent you, *The Other Side of the Story*, about the mitzvah of judging people favorably? I'll bet we can think of a hundred excuses for Irving."

"Like what?"

"Maybe he's sick and needs to get to the hospital."

"Come on! He was doing sixty miles an hour after that cab. He's healthier than Arnold Schwartzenweis."

"Maybe his wife is having a baby."

"She had one last week."

"Maybe he needs to visit her in the hospital."

"She's home."

"Maybe he's running to the hospital to get a doctor."

"He *is* a doctor."

"Maybe he needs supplies from the hospital."

"The hospital is a three-minute walk in the opposite direction."

"Well, maybe he forgot it's Shabbos!"

"Of course he knows it's Shabbos. Didn't you see his tie? His paisley beige 100% silk Giovani tie from Italy. He never wears it during the week."

"Wow, you're really observant! I didn't even notice he was wearing a tie."

"How could you not notice? Didn't you see how it was caught on the back fender of the taxi?"

title: The Seeing Eye Chihuahua
text: One Shabbat morning Abe and Hymie are walking their dogs past the shul. "Let's go in," says Abe. "I hear they have really good chopped liver at the Kiddush." "They'll never let us in with the dogs," says Hymie. "Just follow my lead," says Abe, and walks into the synagogue. Sure enough, the shammas tells him, "No dogs allowed." "But it's my seeing-eye dog," Abe replies. "Sorry, I didn't know," says the shammas. "OK, you can go in." Hymie follows, and again the shammas says, "No dogs allowed." "But it's my seeing-eye dog," says Hymie. The shammas looks at him. "This is your seeing-eye dog? A Chihuahua?" Hymie looks startled. "Is *that* what they gave me?"

title: Now It's 3 to 2
text: Four rabbis had a long series of theological arguments, and three of them were always in agreement against the fourth. One day, after the usual "three to one, majority rules" that meant he had lost again, the odd rabbi out decided to appeal to a higher authority. "Oh, G-d!" he cried. "I know in my heart that I am right and they are wrong! Please give me a sign to prove it to them!" It was a beautiful, sunny day. As soon as the rabbi finished his prayer, a storm cloud moved across the sky above the four. It rumbled once and dissolved. "A sign from G-d! See, I'm right, I knew it!" But the other three disagreed, pointing out that storm clouds form on hot days. So the rabbi prayed again: "Oh, G-d, I need a bigger sign to show that I am right and they are wrong. Please, G-d, a bigger sign!" This time four storm clouds appeared, rushed together into one big cloud, and a bolt of lightning struck a tree on a nearby hill. "I told you I was right!" cried the rabbi, but his friends insisted that nothing had happened that couldn't be explained by natural causes. The rabbi was getting ready to ask for a very big sign, but just as he said "Oh, G-d..." the sky turned pitch black, the earth shook, and a deep, booming voice intoned, "HE'S RIIIGHT!" The rabbi put his hands on his hips and turned to the other three. "Well?" "So," shrugged one of them, "now it's three to two."

title: The Haysidonder
text: A little old Jewish man came home from Shabbos services with a huge smile on his face. His wife remarked how happy he looked and asked what had happened. He told her that after years of service to the synagogue, they had finally given him an official position of importance. "Did they make you president of the brotherhood?" she asked. "No. Better!" "President of the synagogue?" "No, better!" "President of the board of trustees?" "No, better!" Exasperated, she asked, "So what position did they give you?" "They made me the Haysidonder!" His wife was puzzled. "I've never heard of such a position." He explained that it is one of the most important positions anyone can have, especially on the High Holidays. "I stand in the back just as the rabbi is about to start his sermon, and if anyone stands up and tries to leave, I get to yell out: 'Hey! Sid down dere!'"

title: I Won't Bother You Again
text: Two fishermen were out at sea when a terrible storm blew up out of nowhere. It looked as though they were about to capsize, with very little hope of surviving. One fisherman said to the other, "We'd better start praying!" "What do you mean, pray?" said the other. "I haven't prayed to G-d in years!" "Well, you'd better do some praying now, because we need a miracle to save us from drowning!" So this was his prayer: "Dear G-d, I know I haven't talked to You in fifteen years, but if You get me back on dry land alive, I promise that for the next fifteen years I won't bother You again!"

title: The Way to Shul
text: Yossy was waiting outside the Pick 'n Pay for his mother when a man came up to him. "Good morning, young man. Can you tell me where the post office is?" "Sure!" said Yossy. "Go straight down this street a couple of blocks and turn right." The man thanked him kindly and said, "I'm the new rabbi in town. I'd like you to come to shul on Shabbos. I'll show you how to get to Heaven." Yossy laughed. "That's a bubbe maiseh, right? You don't even know the way to the post office!"

title: We're Mishpocha
text:
A man is out in the woods when he comes across a bear. Frightened for his life, he runs as fast as he can and hides in a cave. To his horror, the bear has followed him in, and now he is trapped. He closes his eyes and begins to recite the Shema, expecting his final moments.

When he finishes, he opens his eyes and is astonished to see the bear in front of him with its eyes closed, also praying. The man thinks to himself, "How lucky am I to be cornered by what must be the only Jewish bear in the world! We're mishpocha. I'm saved!" Then he listens more carefully to the bear's prayer: "...hamotzi lechem min ha'aretz."

title: A Nice Jewish Home
text: After the bris of his baby brother in shul, little Chaim sobbed all the way home in the back seat of the car. His father asked him three times what was wrong. Finally the boy replied, "That rabbi said he wanted us brought up in a nice Jewish home, and I want to stay with you guys!"

title: The Tenth Man
text:
Picture the scene: a small town in the West, the hottest day ever. A giant of a man, six foot eight, strides into the saloon, walks up to the counter, bangs his fist on it and growls, "I hear there's a Jew in this bar." No reply. He bangs his fist again: "I hear there's a Jew in this saloon."

In one of the alcoves, little Chaim starts trembling. "Oy," he thinks, "what do I do now? Why does he want me? How does he even know I'm here?" A third time the fist comes down. "For the last time, where's the Jew in this bar?" growls the giant.

Chaim decides to own up. "S-s-s-sir, I'm Chaim, the Jew you're looking for." The giant turns around, looks Chaim straight in the eye and says, softly, "Chaim, why didn't you come out the first time? Come, quickly, we need you for a minyan. We're about to daven Mincha."

title: You Must Have a Great Oven
text:
As a professional photographer, Judy Salzberg takes a lot of pride in her pictures. Wherever she goes, she brings them along to show off her work. She and her husband Harold were invited to the Epsteins for Shabbat dinner, and Judy brought her pictures. "Wow," said Mrs. Epstein, "these are really nice pictures. You must have a great camera."

Fuming at the implication that her whole talent came from her camera, Judy waited until the end of the meal and then thanked her hostess: "Thank you, the Shabbos meal was delicious." And then, as if as an afterthought, she added, "You must have a great oven."

title: Praying I Can Do Myself
text: Naomi, Becky and Joy visited their friend Gittel, a mother of four, who was laid up with a bad back. "Oy, such a shame," exclaimed Naomi. "I know," agreed Becky. "The pain, and now the operation. Such tsuris." "Darling," said Joy, as the other women nodded, "we'll pray for you every night!" Said Gittel, "Wash my dishes. Praying I can do myself."

title: Shaina Punim Kenahora Poo-Poo-Poo
text: A grandmother and her cute little granddaughter went to the mall. While shopping, they became separated. A security guard saw the sobbing little girl and asked her name. She responded, "Shaina-Punim-Kenahora-Poo-Poo-Poo." He asked again, and again she said, "My name is Shaina-Punim-Kenahora-Poo-Poo-Poo." So he announced over the PA that he had a cute brown-eyed, brown-haired little girl who had lost her grandma, and would she please come to the information center to claim "Shaina-Punim-Kenahora-Poo-Poo-Poo." Ten grandmas came running to claim her!

title: Leviticus Chapter 28
text: One Shabbos, Rabbi Bloom told his congregation, "Next week my sermon will be all about the sin of lying. To help you understand it better, I would like you all to read Leviticus chapter 28 before next week." The following Shabbos, at the start of his sermon, Rabbi Bloom asked, "How many of you have read Leviticus 28?" Every hand went up. Rabbi Bloom smiled and said, "Leviticus has only 27 chapters. I will now proceed with my sermon on the sin of lying."

title: It's Shabbos on Mars
text:
Two astronauts land on Mars. Their mission: to check whether there is oxygen on the planet. "Give me the box of matches," says one. "Either it burns and there is oxygen, or nothing happens." He takes the box and is ready to strike a match when, out of the blue, a Martian appears, waving all his arms: "No, no, don't!"

The two look at each other, worried. Could there be an unknown explosive gas on Mars? Still, he takes out another match, and a crowd of hysterical Martians comes running, all waving their arms: "No, no, don't do that!" One astronaut says, "This looks serious. What are they afraid of? Nonetheless, we're here for science, to find out if man can breathe on Mars." So he strikes the match. It flares up, burns down, and nothing happens!

He turns to the Martians and asks, "Why did you want to stop us from striking a match?" The leader of the Martians says, "It's Shabbos!"

title: He's No Chazan
text:
A girl comes to her father and announces her marriage plans. When the father asks the boy's occupation, she tells him that he is a chazan. The father says, "No daughter of mine will marry a chazan!" The girl and her mother cry and beg, but the father is adamant; he won't consider a chazan for his daughter. Finally they convince him to go to shul and hear the prospective chasan in action.

After the davening, the father comes to his daughter and wishes her mazel tov. The daughter, delirious with joy, asks what changed his mind about her intended. He replies, "I heard him, and he's no chazan!"

title: How Many Can You Sleep?
text: A man walks by a new shul he's thinking of joining. He sees someone out front and starts a conversation. "Excuse me, the rabbi's sermons are extremely important to me. Could you perhaps give them a rating?" "I'm sorry, my good friend, but actually I'm the chazan here. It just wouldn't be right for me to comment." "All right. At least, then, could you tell me about the attendance? How large a crowd do you get?" "Oh, on a good Shabbos we can sleep 350."

title: Undivided Attention
text:
A wealthy, successful businessman needed a large sum of money, millions of dollars, for his latest venture. When the money was not forthcoming from the usual sources, when the banks and financial institutions refused to help and the deadline for the deal was fast approaching, he decided to turn to the lender of last resort: Hashem.

He entered the synagogue, stood before the Holy Ark and poured out his heart to the Almighty. "I need so many million dollars, and in a hurry," he pleaded.

Suddenly he noticed that next to him stood another Jew, a poor man asking Hashem for a few dollars to put bread on the table for his large and growing family. The businessman took out his wallet, pulled out a hundred-dollar bill and handed it to the poor man, who left the shul overjoyed at his good fortune.

The businessman then returned to his place and addressed the Almighty: "May I now please have Your undivided attention?"

title: One Short of a Minyan
text:
Early one morning, as Patrick and John are walking past the Great Portland Street Shul, Patrick asks, "So how many people do you think are in this big synagogue, John?"

"There are exactly nine hundred and ninety-nine thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine people in there," replies John.

"Wow!" says Patrick. "How on earth do you know that?"

"Because yesterday morning," John replies, "I heard one of them come out and tell a passer-by that they were one short of a million."

title: Ritually Challenged
text:
In a big Conservative shul in Toronto there was once a president who was a fine businessman but, Jewishly speaking, a bit ritually challenged.

On Rosh Hashanah the gabbai offered him an aliyah. Panicked, he said, "No, no, no. I can't read the Hebrew blessings. I'll embarrass myself."

"You have to take some honor," said the gabbai. "You're the president!"

"Isn't there anything where I don't have to talk?"

The gabbai thought for a minute and suggested, "How about gelilah?"

"What's gelilah?" asked the president.

"Simple," replied the gabbai. "You come up after the Torah is lifted, and when the cover is put on, you put on the breastplate and the crown, and then you sit down."

Relieved, the president accepted the honor. And so, right after hagbah, the lifting of the Torah, the president came up, put on the breastplate and the crown, and went back to his seat.

The gabbai came running over: "On the Torah! On the Torah!"

title: It's the Receipt That Counts
text:
Joe Greenberg was one of the wealthiest men in town. To every charitable organization that called him, knocked on his door or sent him an appeal letter, he always had the same response: "Soon, soon. Don't worry, you'll see." Month after month, year after year, Joe grew wealthier, but his answer never changed: "Soon, soon. Don't worry, you'll see."

At a ripe old age, Joe finally passed away. He never did make good on any of his half-hearted promises. In fact, he never gave a penny to charity in his whole life.

When he arrived at the gates of Heaven, the guardians examined his list of good deeds. "What about all these 'soon, soons' and 'you'll sees' you told the charities, synagogues and yeshivas?" they asked.

"No problem," said Joe, calmly pulling out his checkbook and writing checks to every single organization that had ever approached him. "I'll make good on everything right away," he declared confidently.

"Sorry," said the angel. "Up here we only accept receipts."

title: Mr. Bloom's Prayer
text:
Mr. Bloom is davening in shul with real fervor: "Please, G-d, I desperately need a hundred pounds. Please send it to me." His rabbi overhears him. The rabbi has only half the amount, but even though it is not the full hundred, he decides to give it to Mr. Bloom to help him.

The next day Mr. Bloom finds an envelope with fifty pounds and a note from the rabbi saying the money is for him. He prays to G-d: "Thank You for the money. But next time, don't send it through the rabbi. The ganef kept half!"

title: The Cowboy and the Sermon
text:
One Shabbat a cowboy went to shul. When he walked in, he saw that he and the rabbi were the only ones there. The rabbi asked the cowboy whether he should go ahead and give the sermon anyway. The cowboy said, "I'm not a very learned man, but if I went out to feed my cattle and only one showed up, I'd feed him."

So the rabbi began his sermon. One hour passed, then two, then two and a half. When the rabbi finally finished, he came down and asked the cowboy how he had liked the sermon.

The cowboy answered, "Well, I'm not a very learned man, but if I went out to feed my cattle and only one showed up, I sure wouldn't feed him all the hay."

title: The Manischewitz Account
text:
The CEO of Empire Kosher Chicken was visiting the rabbi of a prominent synagogue. After talking for almost an hour, the CEO finally brought up what he had come to ask. "Rabbi," he said, "I'm willing to give this synagogue five million dollars. But before I do, I must ask that the traditional blessing made over wine on Shabbat be changed to a blessing over chicken."

The rabbi was taken aback. "For thousands of years we have been making the blessing over wine," he told the CEO, "and now, in one short moment, you want me to go against this age-old tradition? I don't think I can do this."

The CEO was undaunted. "Rabbi, you drive a hard bargain. All right, I'll give you ten million dollars to do this. But not a penny more."

The rabbi looked at the CEO and, after several moments, replied, "I'll have to get back to you on that."

The CEO left, and the rabbi promptly called a meeting of the synagogue's board of directors. When all the members had arrived, the rabbi stood up to speak. "Gentlemen, I have some good news and some bad news." The members knew something big was up; the rabbi always began this way when a major undertaking was at hand.

"We have just come into ten million dollars!" The board gasped at the figure, and the excitement grew. "That's the good news," the rabbi went on. "The bad news is, we just lost the Manischewitz account."

title: Does Hashem Always Answer?
text:
The rabbi's son once asked, "Daddy, I notice that every Shabbos morning, before you give your sermon, you kiss the Aron Kodesh where the Torah scrolls are kept. What are you doing?"

Rabbi Rosenberg explained, "I'm davening to Hashem that He should let me give a good sermon."

"Hmm," thought Chaim. "So Hashem doesn't always answer our prayers?"

title: Return of the Credit Card
text: Today was the day Rochel had been waiting for: her wedding day. At the start of the ceremony, her father escorts her down the aisle to the chuppah. She looks absolutely stunning, and all eyes are on her. They reach the chosson, and just before her father steps away, Rochel smiles and places something in his hand. Those in the front row see what it is and begin to laugh quietly. In return for giving his daughter away in marriage, she has given her father back his credit card.

title: Adam's Suit
text:
Little Moishie opened his Zaidy's old Chumash, which he had been told had been in the family for years. Fascinated, he turned the old pages one by one. Then something fell out of the Chumash. He picked it up and looked at it closely: an old leaf from a tree, pressed between the pages.

"Zaidy, look what I found!" Moishie called out.

"What is it, Moishie?" his Zaidy asked.

With astonishment in his voice, young Moishie answered, "It's Adam's suit!"

title: Hagbah
text:
Moshe, a newcomer in shul, is asked to do Hagbah. It is a pitiful sight: he can barely lift the Sefer Torah, almost drops it, and sits down very quickly. Embarrassed, he resolves to go home and work out. For the next few months he lifts weights and does push-ups, sit-ups and pull-ups. He is ready.

The next Shabbos Moshe comes to shul excited and ready. Suddenly he hears the gabbai call his name. He rushes up to the bimah, grabs the Sefer Torah, lifts it and opens it to at least ten columns, swinging it to the left and to the right. He is feeling very proud.

He turns to the gabbai and asks, "So, how was it?" The gabbai says, "Well, your Hagbah was great, but I called you up for Maftir."

title: Why Do You Go to Shul?
text:
Harry called up his old friend Berny. "Can we meet Saturday morning?"

"I'm busy," says Berny.

"What are you up to?"

"I go to shul now on Saturday mornings!"

"Really? You? You go to shul?" asks Harry. "You're an atheist! And you're on a diet, so you can't even enjoy the Kiddush."

"I'll tell you," says Berny. "You remember our friend Yankel Miller? Rumor has it that he started going to shul on Shabbos morning, and he became a billionaire. So I also started going to shul on Saturday mornings."

"Really, Berny? And what do you do in shul? You talk to G-d? You don't even believe He exists!"

"No," says Berny. "Never! That's what Yankel does in shul. He talks to G-d. I go to shul to talk to Yankel!"

title: Three Days a Year
text:
The story is told of a rabbi who came to speak to the cheder class about Rosh Hashanah. Behind his back he held a shofar. "Who can guess what I have behind my back?" he asked the children. "I'll give you a clue: you only find it in shul on three days of the year."

"That's easy," replied one of the kids. "It's my Dad!"

title: Somebody Called Rashi
text:
David Rosenberg was a collector of rare Jewish books. One day he ran into his old friend Chaim Yankel, who told him he had just thrown away an old Hebrew Bible he had found in a dusty old box.

"You threw it out?! You can't do that!" scolded the collector. "Just how old was it?"

"Really old," answered Chaim Yankel. "Like, really old. It could be as much as a thousand years old, who knows?"

"Are you crazy?! First of all, you can't throw away a Chumash, it's sacred!" said the furious collector. "Second, an old Chumash could be worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to the right collector. Oh my G-d, what have you done?!"

"Oh, don't worry," replied Chaim Yankel. "I don't think this book would have been worth anything close to that. There were Hebrew notes scribbled all over the margins."

Now even more alarmed, the collector asked, "Scribbles? Any idea who wrote them?"

"My Hebrew's not that great, but it looked like somebody called Rashi."

title: Hashem Is Watching the Apples
text: The school bell rang and the children ran down to the lunchroom. The Jewish day school was having a special lunch, with treats the parents had brought in as a fundraiser for the school. At the start of the lunch line stood a basket full of apples. Next to it a teacher had placed a little card: "Take only one. Hashem is watching." Farther down the line was a big plate of cookies, already half empty. Propped against the plate was a small piece of paper, in a child's sloppy handwriting: "TAKE AS MANY AS YOU WANT. HASHEM IS WATCHING THE APPLES."

title: Baruch Hashem and Shema Yisrael
text:
A Jewish rider bought a horse from a fellow Jew. The horse was a perfect specimen, but it had been trained in a peculiar way: it would only run at the command "Baruch Hashem" and only stop at the command "Shema Yisrael." The buyer memorized the code and bade the seller farewell. With a loud "Baruch Hashem" he dug his heels into the horse's sides and took off at a gallop.

The problem became clear very quickly: he couldn't remember the code to stop the horse. He tried everything he could think of. "Good Shabbos!" "Shanah Tovah!" Nothing worked. The horse was climbing a cliff, and he knew that in seconds he would sail over the edge to his death. Desperately he tried to remember the code, but couldn't. Staring death in the face, he closed his eyes and cried out what every Jew cries on his deathbed: "Shema Yisrael!" The horse skidded to a stop right at the edge of the cliff.

The rider hesitantly opened his eyes and looked down. Shocked at how close he had come to death, he shouted out, "Baruch Hashem!"

title: I Knew I Could Count on You
text:
Hymie goes to see his boss and says, "We're doing some house-cleaning at home tomorrow for Pesach, and my wife needs me to help with the cleaning and the shlepping, moving and hauling stuff."

"We're short-handed, Hymie," the boss replies. "I just can't give you the day off."

"Thanks, boss," says Hymie. "I knew I could count on you!"

title: Hit Him Again
text: A crumbling old synagogue building needed remodeling, so during his sermon the rabbi made an impassioned appeal, looking directly at the richest man in town. At the end of the sermon the rich man stood up and announced, "Rabbi, I will contribute $1,000." Just then, plaster fell from the ceiling and struck him on the shoulder. He promptly stood back up and shouted, "Rabbi, I will increase my donation to $5,000!" Before he could sit down, plaster fell on him again, and again he practically screamed, "Rabbi, I will double my last pledge!" He sat down, and a larger chunk of plaster fell on his head. He stood up once more and hollered, "Rabbi, I will give $20,000!" At which the cantor shouted, "Hit him again, G-d! Hit him again!"

title: Foreign Language
text:
A group of guys I know took a trip to France and decided to attend the Chabad House in a small town, even though none of them understood French. They weren't the most regular shul-goers even at home, and it was even harder to follow the service in a foreign language, so they decided to stand and sit whenever the rest of the congregation did. At one point the rabbi spoke, and the man sitting next to them stood up, so they got up too. The entire congregation broke into hearty laughter.

After the service they approached the shliach, who spoke English, and asked him what had been so funny. The rabbi said he had announced a birth and asked the father to stand up.

title: I Must Have Been Really Sick
text:
A man who was very sick, and obviously frightened, said to his rabbi, "Pray for me, and if I get well, I'll donate $25,000 to the synagogue building fund."

Several months later the rabbi met him on the street. "How are you?" he asked.

"Just marvelous, Rabbi," the man replied.

"I've been meaning to speak to you," the rabbi continued, "about that money for the synagogue."

"What are you talking about?"

"You asked me to pray for you, and said that if you got well you would donate $25,000 to the fund for the new synagogue."

"If I said that," the former patient exclaimed, "then I really must have been sick."

title: A Sign from Heaven
text: After starting a new diet, I changed my route to the gym so I wouldn't pass my favorite bakery. This morning I accidentally drove by it, and as I approached, there in the window was a whole host of goodies. I felt this was no accident, so I prayed: "L-rd, it's up to You. If You want me to have any of those delicious goodies, make a parking place for me right in front of the bakery." And sure enough, He answered my prayer: on the eighth time around the block, there it was.

title: How to Stay Safe in Today's World
text:
How to stay safe in today's world:

1. Avoid riding in automobiles: they are responsible for 20% of all fatal accidents.
2. Do not stay at home: 17% of all accidents occur in the home. (That's 37% already.)
3. Avoid walking on streets or sidewalks: 14% of all accidents happen to pedestrians. (Now we're up to 51%.)
4. Avoid traveling by air, rail or water: 16% of all accidents involve these forms of transportation. (That brings us to 67%.)
5. Of the remaining 33%, 32% of all deaths occur in hospitals. Above all else, avoid hospitals.

Now, you will be pleased to learn that only 0.01 percent of all deaths occur in a synagogue, and these are usually related to previous physical disorders. Logic therefore tells us that the safest place for you to be at any given moment is in synagogue. Torah study is even safer: the number of deaths during Torah study in synagogue is too small to register statistically. For safety's sake, go to shul as often as possible.

title: Baruch Hashem
text:
In a religious neighborhood of New York, a rabbi left the pulpit to open a business. After working very hard for several years and finally making some money, he decided to buy a new car. As soon as he walked into the local dealership, the salesman spotted him. "Have I got a car for you!" he exclaimed, unable to hide his delight at finding an obviously religious man.

The rabbi-turned-businessman, in his dark suit and long beard, looked at the salesman with apprehension. "What do you mean?"

"Ah ha," said the salesman, rubbing his hands together. "Let me show you the latest technological advance: an American car with Israeli-designed computerized digital commands. One of a kind, I tell you. You won't believe your eyes." He opened the door of the shiny new sedan. "Please sit down. You see, this car has no pedals. That's right: no gas pedal and no brake pedal."

"B-but how do you stop and start?"

"Ah, that's the beauty of it. With the Israeli computerized technology, all you have to do is speak, and the digital processor turns your voice into an electronic signal that tells the motor what to do. It was programmed for the religious consumer. To start, just say 'Baruch Hashem.'" As the salesman spoke those words, the car began to drive.

The rabbi was taken aback. "Wow, I don't believe it! How do you stop the car?"

"No problem. All you have to say is 'Shema Yisrael' and the car will stop." As he spoke those words, the car rolled to a halt. "It's as easy as can be: 'Baruch Hashem' to start, and when you want to stop, 'Shema Yisrael.'"

The rabbi was very impressed and bought the car on the spot. He got in, said the magic words, "Baruch Hashem," and the car was soon heading out onto the highway. Before long he had left the city behind and was gazing at the beautiful countryside. As the car went on, the rabbi failed to notice a sign saying the road was closed, and the car drove up onto a half-finished bridge. "Oh no! We're going to crash!" Instinctively his feet searched for the brake pedal, but there was none.

"What do I say? WHAT DO I SAY?!" In his panic he could not remember what the salesman had told him. His mind was blank, and the car was nearing the end of the unfinished bridge and a majestic plunge into a ravine hundreds of feet below. "This is the end," the rabbi thought. Preparing for death, he began to declare the unity of G-d: "Shema Yisrael!" In a moment the car screeched to a stop, half of it tilted precariously over the edge of the bridge.

The rabbi, soaked with sweat, said, "Baruch Hashem!!"

title: Mervyn's Bar Mitzvah Aliyah
text:
Mervyn is invited to his nephew's Bar Mitzvah. The invitation also says they would like him to have an aliyah. Not being a regular shul-goer, he learns how to recite the brachah. Every day he practices: "Barchu et Hashem hamevorach... Baruch Hashem hamevorach l'olam va'ed." The day before the Bar Mitzvah he practices it several more times, and when he goes to sleep that night he is confident he knows it well.

The day of the Bar Mitzvah arrives, and soon it is time for his aliyah. He goes up to the bimah and says, "Barchu et Hashem hamevorach." Everyone behind him answers, "Baruch Hashem hamevorach l'olam va'ed."

"SHUT UP!" he shouts. "I can do it myself!"

title: Something We Have in Excess
text:
One Friday night I was in the synagogue and the rabbi was giving his usual sermon. At the end he told the congregation, "Before we continue, I'd like to let you know that our synagogue has decided to collect goods for the neediest people in our area. It's for a good cause and we need your help. Please bring us this Sunday anything lying around your house that you can spare or have no great need for. I'm sure you can all think of something you have in excess."

Behind me I heard an old lady say to the neighbor sitting next to her, "Yes. Tzores..."

title: Who Wants to Go to Heaven?
text:
Rabbi Epstein was a particularly tenacious clergyman, and he couldn't stand seeing Jewish people getting drunk. So one day he went into a tavern frequented by Jewish patrons. He walked in and saw Stan from shul. "Stan, do you want to go to heaven?"

"I do, Rabbi."

"Then stand over there against the wall."

Then Rabbi Epstein asked another man he recognized, "Do you want to go to heaven?"

"Certainly, Rabbi."

"Then stand over there against the wall."

Then Rabbi Epstein walked up to Chaim Yankel Rabbinowitz. "Do you want to go to heaven?"

"No, I don't, Rabbi."

The rabbi was in disbelief. "You mean to tell me that when you die, you don't want to go to heaven?"

"Oh, when I die, yes," said Chaim Yankel. "I thought you were getting a group together to go right now."

title: The Weird Jews
text: This month I blew a ram's horn, ate a fish head, swung a chicken around my head, dressed in a suit and sneakers, then wore a white robe and prayed and fasted for 25 hours, built and ate in a tent with a bamboo ceiling (sometimes in the rain), spent three days in a row with my in-laws and three more with my parents, walked around with a palm branch and a citrus fruit, whipped willow branches on the floor, ate roughly 8 kg of meat, used six vacation days without leaving my neighborhood, and spent almost as much time in shul as I do in my office.

title: I Live in Cape Town
text:
There is a story about an SAA flight from London to Johannesburg. Shortly before it was due to land, the captain announced that because of bad weather in Johannesburg the flight was being diverted to Cape Town. A stewardess saw a man with a beard and a yarmulke take a small book with strange characters from his pocket and begin to intone prayers. "Silly man," she thought, "does he think his prayers will clear the weather over Johannesburg?" But just a few minutes later the captain announced that the weather over Johannesburg had improved and they would be landing there after all.

Filled with remorse, the stewardess approached the man. "Sir, I owe you an apology. When the captain made his first announcement and I saw you start to pray, I doubted whether your prayers would help the weather. Obviously they did. Please accept my apologies."

The man answered, "There's no need to apologize, young lady. My prayers were not for the weather. You see, I live in Cape Town!"

title: Are You Starting Again?
text:
Two men were always fighting. Finally, before Yom Kippur, the rabbi got them together, and they hugged, kissed and made up. After Ne'ilah one says to the other, "I davened that you should have all the things you davened for me."

"Are you trying to start up again?"

title: Ten Inches of Water
text:
A boy was sitting on a park bench with one hand resting on an open Bible, loudly praising G-d. "Hallelujah! Hallelujah! G-d is great!" he shouted, without caring whether anyone heard him.

Along came a man who had recently finished some studies at the local university. Feeling very enlightened in the ways of truth, and eager to show it, he asked the boy the reason for his joy.

"Don't you have any idea what G-d can do?" said the boy. "I just read that G-d opened the waves of the Red Sea and led the whole nation of Israel right through the middle."

The enlightened man laughed lightly, sat down next to the boy and set about opening his eyes to the "realities" of the miracles of the Bible. "That can all be very easily explained. Modern scholarship has shown that the Red Sea in that area was only ten inches deep at the time. It was no problem for the Israelites to wade across."

The boy was stumped. His eyes wandered from the man back to the Bible open in his lap. The man, satisfied that he had enlightened a poor, naive young person to the finer points of scientific insight, turned to go.

He had scarcely taken two steps when the boy began to rejoice and praise louder than before. The man turned to ask the reason. "Wow!" exclaimed the boy happily. "G-d is greater than I thought! Not only did He lead the whole nation of Israel through the Red Sea, He topped it off by drowning the whole Egyptian army in ten inches of water!"
